title: Trace replay & microbenchmark correlation notes
content:
Purpose:
This note records the trace-replay microbenchmark experiments we ran to investigate a persistent p99 gap between production traces and our synthetic bench results. Goal: find why synthetic microbenchmarks underpredict tail latency seen in production traces and produce actionable hypotheses and short remediation steps.

Background/context:
- Problem: Production E2E traces (sampled over last 30 days) show median-ok but p99 ~2.2x higher than our synthetic loadbench for the same throughput and payload distribution.
- Suspected contributors: kernel-level stalls, OS scheduling/NUMA behavior under mixed workloads, rare long attention steps (large seqlen spikes), and contention in request-level batching code.
- Approach: build a trace-replay harness that replays sampled trace arrivals (inter-arrival times and payload seeds) against the runtime in an isolated environment while capturing the same per-stage trace hooks (ingest, deserialize, routing, batching-wait, model-kernel, kv-lookup, emit, egress). Then run microbenchmarks that exercise individual stages to correlate stage timings with spikes in production tails.

Trace set & selection:
- Source: daily-sampled production traces (trace ids: sample set P30-202601) filtered to requests with model variant rv2-small and response lengths between 16–512 tokens.
- Chosen cohorts: 1) Stable short sequences (16–64 tokens), 2) Mixed sequences with occasional long tails (16–512 tokens, heavy right tail), 3) High-concurrency small requests (many concurrent short requests).

Replay harness configuration (short):
- Harness: trace-replay-v2 (local cluster build), pinned to kernel image k8s-node-2025-12-18 to match production kernel/driver versions.
- Concurrency: replicates observed 95th percentile in-flight requests per-cell.
- Payload seeding: deterministic token shapes to preserve KV cache hit/miss patterns.
- Instrumentation: same trace spans and per-stage timers as production (added microsecond resolution where missing), logged to local parquet traces for offline analysis.

Microbenchmark scenarios run:
1) Baseline synthetic bench: constant payload shape, fixed inter-arrival poisson, no seqlen spikes.
2) Replay of real arrival patterns (inter-arrival + seqlen distribution) with full runtime instrumentation.
3) Isolated kernel bench: run busy-loop synthetic workload inside model-kernel stage to stress GPU kernel launch and measure tail related to kernel queue depth.
4) Blocking I/O bench: insert artificial randomized 1–10ms delays in egress path to check egress backpressure effects on batching/wait times.
5) NUMA/smt variant bench: toggle cpuset/numa-bind and run the replay to surface scheduling-induced latency jumps.

Key aggregated results (single run summaries) — cohort: mixed sequences (most diagnostic)
- Baseline synthetic bench (no trace replay): p50=32ms, p95=78ms, p99=120ms.
- Trace replay (same cluster config): p50=35ms, p95=95ms, p99=258ms.
- Kernel bench (high kernel queue): p50=33ms, p95=110ms, p99=210ms.
- Blocking I/O injected (random 1–10ms): p50=37ms, p95=140ms, p99=300ms.
- NUMA off (no binding): p50=34ms, p95=102ms, p99=240ms.

Per-stage median/p95/p99 breakdown (trace-replay run; numbers in ms):
- Ingest (parse headers + auth): median=1.2, p95=3.5, p99=8.1
- Deserialize/prepare prompt: median=2.4, p95=7.8, p99=18.3
- Routing & policy check: median=0.9, p95=2.6, p99=6.4
- Batching-wait (time spent queued waiting for batch formation): median=4.6, p95=26.3, p99=134.7
- KV-cache lookup & cold miss overhead: median=0.5, p95=3.1, p99=22.6
- Model kernel execution (incl kernel-queue wait): median=12.7, p95=28.9, p99=96.2
- Emit & serialization: median=1.1, p95=3.9, p99=11.0
- Egress (network send + TLS): median=2.0, p95=5.4, p99=18.2

Observations & diagnostic correlations:
1) Batching-wait tail dominates the replay p99. Batch formation time p99 is 134ms vs median 4.6ms — indicates rare long waits where a request sits unbatched for multiple collection cycles. These line up with times when rare long-seqlen requests are in-flight and aggregate batch size is reduced.
2) Kernel queueing contributes strongly to p95–p99. The kernel bench reproduced a similar p99 when synthetic kernel queue depth was increased.
3) Injected small egress I/O delays amplify batching-wait and kernel queue tails due to backpressure — a 1–10ms jitter produces a ~20–30% increase in p99 in replay.
4) KV-cache cold misses appear in p99 (22.6ms spikes) but are not the main driver of the observed gap.
5) NUMA/scheduler effects: running without strict CPU/NUMA binding increases p99 by ~15–20% in our bench — suggests OS-level noise matters for tails in mixed-workload cells.

Hypotheses (ranked):
- H1: Rare long-seqlen requests reduce effective batching efficiency and increase per-request batching-wait, causing the bulk of p99 gap.
- H2: Small amplification from egress and serialization jitter creates backpressure that cascades into both batching and kernel queues, turning small jitter into large tail events.
- H3: Kernel scheduling and driver-level preemption on host nodes occasionally stalls kernel dispatch long enough to show up in p99.
- H4: NUMA misbinding and OS scheduling noise are second-order contributors but measurable and actionable.

Repro tips & artifacts to inspect:
- Inspect trace span id X-REPLAY-xxxx for examples with batching-wait > 200ms and correlate with seqlen field in request metadata.
- Use trace-replay-v2 config 'preserve-kv-seed=true' to ensure KV miss patterns match production sample for more accurate cold-miss reproduction.
- For kernel queue reproductions, use gpu-kernel-sim harness at QD=8 and sample kernel-start timestamps to see queueing histograms.

Short-term mitigations (quick wins):
- Add a batching policy that caps maximum batching-wait contribution for requests tagged as latency-sensitive; fall back to smaller-batch fast-path if wait exceeds threshold (~40ms).
- Rate-limit or isolate very long-seqlen requests into separate lanes (dedicated pool or lower-priority queue) to avoid contaminating short-request latency.
- Harden egress path with smaller socket write buffers and prioritize critical control plane messages to reduce jitter propagation.

Medium-term work (next 1–2 sprints):
- Implement dynamic batching heuristics that consider in-flight seqlen distribution and can adapt collector window sizes to avoid pathological waits for low-frequency long requests.
- Pilot kernel queue metrics in exporter (per-GPU queue depth + dispatch latency) and add SLO alarms targeting p99 kernel-dispatch time.
- Validate NUMA/cpuset recommendations for our node images and add recommended node profile for latency-sensitive pods.

Longer-term investigations:
- Explore preemptible kernel splitting: allow long-running kernels to be preempted or segmented to reduce head-of-queue blocking. Complexity high — research task.
- Evaluate hybrid serving lanes: mix fast small-request optimized runners with slower high-throughput runners and route by request shape.

Immediate action items (owners):
- Priya: push replay harness config preserving KV seeds and run 2 additional 12h replay jobs (due 2026-03-15).
- Ethan: prototype batching fast-path (PR #834 referenced) and run A/B replays (due 2026-03-18).
- María: add kernel-queue exporter prototype to the metrics sidecar and collect QD histograms (due 2026-03-22).

Open questions / unknowns:
- Frequency of underlying root cause in production: are the p99 events concentrated in a small number of nodes or evenly distributed? (need node-level correlation).
- Are there hardware-specific drivers (different GPU generations) that exacerbate kernel queue tails? Current replay used same GPU family but not identical node firmware.
